sections.title: Introduction: The Dimensional Paradox
sections.content: Define the goal: Can a 1D line pass through every single point in a 2D square? Introduce the concept of a 'Space-Filling Curve' as a continuous path that visits every coordinate in a finite area.
sections.example: Visualize a robotic vacuum cleaner trying to clean every inch of a square room by moving in a single, non-overlapping line.

sections.title: The Mechanism: Recursive Construction
sections.content: Explain the prerequisite: Understanding 'Iteration' and 'Fractals'. Show how we start with a simple generator shape and replace every line segment with a scaled-down version of itself infinitely.
sections.example: The Hilbert Curve: Start with a 'U' shape, then replace each side with a smaller 'U' pattern, repeating this process to fill the square density.

sections.title: Visualizing the Mapping (1D to 2D)
sections.content: Demonstrate the mathematical mapping. As the curve reaches 'Infinity' in iterations, the line effectively occupies the space, turning a 1D coordinate into a 2D position (x, y) without leaving gaps.
sections.example: An animation showing a single thread unfolding into a 'Peano Curve' that systematically covers a grid, turning a straight line into a dense 'fabric'.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content: Explain why this matters: Locality. Space-filling curves preserve spatial relationships, making them essential for data indexing and optimization.
sections.example: Database Optimization: Using Z-order curves to store 2D map data in 1D memory, allowing a navigation app to quickly find nearby restaurants by searching only a small segment of the index.

sections.title: Conclusion and Summary
sections.content: Recap: Space-filling curves transform 1D sequences into multidimensional structures. Emphasize that while the line has infinite length, it remains a single continuous path.
sections.example: A final visual of a complex circuit board layout designed using space-filling curves to ensure maximum component density in a tiny device.
